title: Leaving good behind
hookLine: three things keep working after you're gone; and a neighbor's line about treasure
tomorrow: what let one man sleep so well he was promised Paradise?

cards: A playlist someone made years ago that friends still play. A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting, pulled out every holiday. Some things keep working long after the person who made them has stepped away.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim names what keeps working for you after you're gone. When a person dies, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, their deeds come to an end, except for three.

teach.b: The three: a charity that continues, knowledge people benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for him.

Ongoing charity, sadaqa jariya, is good that keeps flowing; teachers give examples like a well, a planted tree, a book on a masjid shelf. Knowledge that benefits is whatever you taught that someone still uses.

And a child who prays for you is love you raised, still saying your name to Allah. All three share one thing: the good keeps moving through people who are still alive, and its reward keeps reaching the one who started it.
Christian neighbors have a line that sits close by.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, in the King James words: "But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt." Both point past the things that rust.
Both say what you give away is what you keep.
And one honest difference: Jesus's picture is treasure stored safe in heaven; the hadith's picture is good still at work on earth.
Neither needs the other to be wrong. Which means a lesson you teach someone can keep counting for you.

how: Muslims give sadaqa jariya, ongoing charity such as wells, schools, trees and books for a masjid, sometimes in the name of someone who has died, and point to this hadith; teaching and raising children who pray are counted in it too.

o: the memories people hold of you after you die
dividing your belongings fairly among your family
good you start that keeps working after you're gone

p: what you taught that someone still uses
treasures in heaven, no moth or rust

s: in Islam, when a person dies, every one of their deeds stops counting
the hadith in Sahih Muslim names three that continue: ongoing charity, useful knowledge, a child who prays.
the hadith counts a righteous child who prays for the parent
love you raised, still saying your name to Allah.
in Matthew, Jesus says to lay up treasures in heaven, where moth and rust don't corrupt
Matthew 6:20, in the King James words.

games.q: your uncle wants to leave something good that keeps working after he's gone. which of these fits the hadith's three most closely?
o: teaching neighborhood kids to read, a skill they keep using.
one huge dinner for the whole masjid, in his name.
a plaque with his name on the masjid's front wall.
games.why: knowledge people benefit from keeps working. a dinner is a good gift, but it ends when the plates are cleared.

practice: Choose one of the three: something you could give that keeps on giving, something you know that you could teach, or someone young you could show up for. Name the first small step and the day you'd take it.
Hold that plan through a few slow breaths.

wordCard.voice: Leaving good behind: giving, teaching and raising love in ways that keep working after you're gone.

orig.note: Arabic: flowing charity, a gift whose good keeps running.

carryVoice: The line for today: what continues, the good still moving through other people. Day five of the journey home, done.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1631: when a person dies, his deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that is benefited from, or a righteous child who prays for him
